lines.text: Welcome to Level 2! Today your functions stop just printing and start giving answers back, like a real calculator.
A parameter is a name inside the brackets of def, like def strike_rate(runs, balls).
When you call the function you pass in values, called arguments.
Inside the function they work just like variables.
return sends a value back to the line that called the function.
You can store it, print it or use it in more maths.
A function with no return gives back None, which means nothing.
Put a formula inside a function and use it for every player. strike_rate(45, 30) and strike_rate(80, 50) run the same code.
Fix a bug once and every use is fixed.
A parameter can have a default value, like overs=20.
If you leave it out when you call the function, Python uses 20.
If you pass a value, your value wins.
This function takes two parameters, the runs and the balls faced.
The return line sends the answer back, and we store it in a variable called sr.
The first function only prints, so it gives nothing back and a holds None.
The second function returns its answer, so b holds the shout and we can use it later.
Five fours and two sixes make thirty-two runs from boundaries.
Because the function returns a number, we can add seven singles straight onto it.
When we leave out the overs, Python uses the default of twenty overs.
When we pass twelve, our value replaces the default for that call.
The function works out the answer, but it never sends it back.
Without the word return, the function gives back None. Add return and you get forty-two.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
